label: A mathematical story from 2000
title: A Langlands bridge over function fields
people: Laurent Lafforgue
explanation: The Langlands program predicts surprising links between equations, symmetry and number systems. In work culminating in 2000, Laurent Lafforgue proved the global Langlands correspondence for general linear groups over function fields, extending an earlier rank-two result of Vladimir Drinfeld.
whyItMatters: The theorem established a vast translation dictionary in one major setting and supplied tools that continue to influence number theory and algebraic geometry.
sourceTitle: Curriculum vitae — Laurent Lafforgue

label: A mathematical story from 2001
title: Cluster algebras grow by mutation
people: Sergey Fomin and Andrei Zelevinsky
explanation: Fomin and Zelevinsky introduced cluster algebras in a paper first submitted in 2001. Starting with a small cluster of variables, one variable at a time is replaced by a precise mutation rule, producing a much larger algebra whose repeated patterns connect combinatorics, geometry and representation theory.
whyItMatters: Cluster algebras created a shared language for structures that had appeared separately across several areas of mathematics.
sourceTitle: Cluster algebras I: Foundations — arXiv

label: A mathematical story from 2002
title: A fast, unconditional test for prime numbers
people: Manindra Agrawal, Neeraj Kayal and Nitin Saxena
explanation: The AKS algorithm determines whether a whole number is prime in a time bounded by a polynomial in the number of its digits. Unlike earlier general-purpose fast tests, it is deterministic and does not depend on an unproved conjecture.
whyItMatters: The result answered a central theoretical-computer-science question with an elegant idea developed at IIT Kanpur.
sourceTitle: PRIMES is in P — Annals of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 2003
title: Ricci flow unlocks three-dimensional space
people: Grigori Perelman, building on Richard Hamilton's Ricci-flow program
explanation: Across three papers posted in 2002 and 2003, Grigori Perelman supplied the missing ideas for controlling singularities in Ricci flow. Mathematicians later verified that the work proves Thurston's geometrization conjecture and therefore the century-old Poincaré conjecture.
whyItMatters: The proof gave topology a powerful way to classify three-dimensional spaces by gradually smoothing their geometry.
sourceTitle: Ricci flow with surgery on three-manifolds — Grigori Perelman

label: A mathematical story from 2004
title: Prime numbers contain patterns of any length
people: Ben Green and Terence Tao
explanation: Green and Tao proved that the prime numbers contain arithmetic progressions of every finite length. For example, 5, 11, 17, 23 and 29 form a five-term progression because the same amount, 6, is added each time.
whyItMatters: The theorem revealed unlimited additive structure inside the primes even though primes become increasingly sparse.
sourceTitle: The primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions — Ben Green and Terence Tao

label: A mathematical story from 2005
title: Software checks every step of the prime number theorem
people: Jeremy Avigad, Kevin Donnelly, David Gray and Paul Raff
explanation: In 2005, Avigad, Donnelly, Gray and Raff described a formal verification of an elementary proof of the prime number theorem using the Isabelle proof assistant. The software did not invent the argument; it checked a carefully encoded chain of definitions and logical steps leading to the theorem that primes near a large number x have density about 1 / ln(x).
whyItMatters: The project showed how proof assistants can make a long mathematical argument precise enough for a computer to verify line by line.
sourceTitle: A formally verified proof of the prime number theorem — arXiv

label: A mathematical story from 2006
title: Sparse signals can be rebuilt from surprisingly few measurements
people: Emmanuel Candès, Justin Romberg, Terence Tao and David Donoho
explanation: Compressed sensing showed that a signal with only a few important components can often be reconstructed exactly from far fewer measurements than its full length suggests. Landmark 2006 papers made this precise using probability, linear algebra and convex optimisation.
whyItMatters: The theory changed how researchers think about sampling and led to practical methods in imaging, astronomy and signal processing.
sourceTitle: Compressed sensing — IEEE Transactions on Information Theory

label: A mathematical story from 2007
title: Ramanujan's mock theta mystery gains a framework
people: Kathrin Bringmann and Ken Ono, building on Sander Zwegers
explanation: Ramanujan left 17 mysterious 'mock theta functions' shortly before his death without a general definition explaining them. Bringmann and Ono used the newer theory of harmonic Maass forms to describe their structure and derive formulas that made many of their hidden properties accessible.
whyItMatters: The work connected an unfinished idea from 1920 to modern number theory, combinatorics and mathematical physics.
sourceTitle: UW scientists unlock major number theory puzzle — University of Wisconsin–Madison

label: A mathematical story from 2008
title: A short polynomial solves finite-field Kakeya
people: Zeev Dvir
explanation: A finite-field Kakeya set contains a full line in every possible direction inside a finite number system. Zeev Dvir proved that such a set must occupy a constant proportion of the whole space, using a strikingly short argument built around a carefully chosen polynomial.
whyItMatters: The proof popularised the polynomial method, which has since unlocked many problems in combinatorics and theoretical computer science.
sourceTitle: On the size of Kakeya sets in finite fields — Zeev Dvir

label: A mathematical story from 2009
title: Most Kervaire-invariant dimensions are ruled out
people: Michael Hill, Michael Hopkins and Douglas Ravenel
explanation: The Kervaire invariant asks whether certain highly unusual smooth shapes can exist in particular dimensions. Hill, Hopkins and Ravenel proved in 2009 that the answer is no beyond a short exceptional list, leaving only dimension 126 undecided at that time.
whyItMatters: Their new machinery resolved almost all of a long-standing problem about high-dimensional manifolds and stable homotopy groups.
sourceTitle: On the non-existence of elements of Kervaire invariant one — Hill, Hopkins and Ravenel

label: A mathematical story from 2010
title: A near-optimal answer to Erdős's distance problem
people: Larry Guth and Nets Hawk Katz
explanation: Place N points anywhere in a plane and count the different distances between pairs. Guth and Katz proved that there must be at least a constant times N divided by log N distinct distances, matching Erdős's predicted power of N apart from the logarithm.
whyItMatters: The proof introduced polynomial partitioning, a technique that now connects geometry, algebra and harmonic analysis.
sourceTitle: On the Erdős distinct distance problem in the plane — Larry Guth and Nets Hawk Katz

label: A mathematical story from 2011
title: A knot that cannot avoid distortion
people: John Pardon
explanation: John Pardon proved that some torus knots cannot be drawn in three-dimensional space without large distortion: for certain pairs of points, travelling along the knot must be far longer than going straight between them. His paper answered a question Mikhail Gromov had asked in 1983 while Pardon was still an undergraduate.
whyItMatters: The result shows that a knot's topology can place unavoidable geometric limits on how efficiently it can sit in space.
sourceTitle: On the distortion of knots on embedded surfaces — Annals of Mathematics

demo.caption: A torus knot winds around the surface of a doughnut-shaped torus.

label: A mathematical story from 2012
title: Perfectoid spaces bridge two arithmetic worlds
people: Peter Scholze
explanation: Peter Scholze introduced perfectoid spaces, mathematical spaces that let researchers translate questions between number systems with very different arithmetic rules. This bridge allowed him to prove new cases of the long-standing weight–monodromy conjecture.
whyItMatters: Perfectoid spaces became a powerful new language in number theory because a hard problem can become tractable after it is moved into the right mathematical world.
sourceTitle: Perfectoid Spaces — Publications Mathématiques de l'IHÉS

label: A mathematical story from 2013
title: Prime numbers can keep close company
people: Yitang Zhang
explanation: Yitang Zhang proved that there are infinitely many pairs of consecutive prime numbers separated by no more than one fixed distance; his first bound was 70 million. This did not prove the twin-prime conjecture, where the gap must be exactly 2, but it was the first proof that some finite gap occurs infinitely often.
whyItMatters: The result broke a major barrier in the study of primes and inspired rapid improvements, including a large online Polymath collaboration.
sourceTitle: Bounded gaps between primes — Annals of Mathematics

demo.caption: The gaps change, but small gaps such as 2 keep returning.

label: A mathematical story from 2014
title: Maryam Mirzakhani makes Fields Medal history
people: Maryam Mirzakhani
explanation: Maryam Mirzakhani became the first woman to receive a Fields Medal. She was honoured for studying curved surfaces and the paths that move across them, making deep connections among geometry, topology and dynamical systems.
whyItMatters: Her work changed how mathematicians understand families of surfaces, while the award marked a historic moment for women in mathematics.
sourceTitle: Fields Medals 2014 — International Mathematical Union

label: A mathematical story from 2015
title: No infinite plus-or-minus pattern stays balanced
people: Terence Tao, building on the Polymath5 collaboration
explanation: Imagine an endless sequence made only from +1 and −1. Terence Tao proved that, whatever pattern is chosen, some regularly spaced selection will have running sums that wander arbitrarily far from zero, settling the Erdős discrepancy problem posed in the 1930s.
whyItMatters: The proof joined number theory, ideas about information and entropy, and earlier crowdsourced work on a question that is simple to state but resisted attack for about 80 years.
sourceTitle: The Erdős discrepancy problem — Terence Tao

demo.caption: Group terms at regular steps and watch how their partial sums change.

label: A mathematical story from 2016
title: The densest packing in eight dimensions
people: Maryna Viazovska
explanation: Maryna Viazovska proved that the highly symmetric E8 arrangement is the densest possible packing of equal spheres in eight-dimensional space. Soon afterward, her method was extended with collaborators to settle the corresponding problem in 24 dimensions.
whyItMatters: A centuries-old packing question yielded to an unexpectedly elegant connection between geometry, Fourier analysis and modular forms.
sourceTitle: The sphere packing problem in dimension 8 — Annals of Mathematics

demo.caption: Packing circles is the two-dimensional analogy; Viazovska proved the optimal answer for spheres in eight dimensions.

label: A mathematical story from 2017
title: High-rank symmetry cannot squeeze into tiny manifolds
people: Aaron Brown, David Fisher and Sebastian Hurtado
explanation: Zimmer's conjecture predicts that sufficiently complicated symmetry groups cannot act in genuinely complicated ways on manifolds that are too small. Brown, Fisher and Hurtado proved major cases for smooth actions of lattices such as finite-index subgroups of SL(m,Z), combining dynamics, geometry and algebra.
whyItMatters: The work establishes a form of mathematical rigidity: below a precise dimension, enormous abstract symmetry has very little room to move.
sourceTitle: Zimmer's conjecture for actions of SL(m,Z) — Brown, Fisher and Hurtado

label: A mathematical story from 2018
title: A classical algorithm catches a quantum one
people: Ewin Tang
explanation: At age 18, Ewin Tang found a classical algorithm for a recommendation problem that ran at a speed comparable to a celebrated quantum algorithm under similar strong data-access assumptions. The result removed one proposed exponential quantum advantage and launched a wider search for quantum-inspired classical algorithms.
whyItMatters: It raised the standard for claims of quantum speedup and showed that studying quantum methods can reveal faster ideas for ordinary computers too.
sourceTitle: A quantum-inspired classical algorithm for recommendation systems — Ewin Tang

label: A mathematical story from 2019
title: The number 42 becomes three cubes
people: Andrew Booker and Andrew Sutherland
explanation: Andrew Booker and Andrew Sutherland used a clever search and a worldwide network of volunteered computers to find three enormous integers whose cubes add to 42. It was the last eligible number below 100 for which no such representation was known; the discovery did not settle the general sum-of-three-cubes problem.
whyItMatters: A school-level equation, x³ + y³ + z³ = 42, hid a search so vast that it required number theory, efficient algorithms and distributed computing.
sourceTitle: Sutherland helps solve decades-old sum-of-three-cubes puzzle — MIT School of Science

label: A mathematical story from 2020
title: The Conway knot is not slice
people: Lisa Piccirillo
explanation: A knot is called smoothly slice if it can form the boundary of a smooth disk when one extra dimension is allowed. Lisa Piccirillo proved that the Conway knot is not slice, closing a question that had resisted every standard test for about 50 years.
whyItMatters: Her indirect method replaced the difficult knot with another knot sharing the right four-dimensional information, giving topology a powerful new way to distinguish shapes.
sourceTitle: The Conway knot is not slice — Annals of Mathematics

demo.caption: The Conway knot has 11 crossings; 'not slice' describes what it cannot bound in four dimensions.

label: A mathematical story from 2020
title: Quantum games reveal an undecidable frontier
people: Zhengfeng Ji, Anand Natarajan, Thomas Vidick, John Wright and Henry Yuen
explanation: The theorem MIP*=RE showed that deciding the best possible outcome of certain games played by entangled quantum provers can encode any computation that eventually halts. As a consequence, there is no algorithm that can correctly calculate the entangled value of every such game, and the result refuted Connes' embedding conjecture.
whyItMatters: One proof unexpectedly connected quantum information, theoretical computer science, operator algebras and the fundamental limits of computation.
sourceTitle: MIP*=RE — Ji, Natarajan, Vidick, Wright and Yuen

label: A mathematical story from 2021
title: New building blocks for number systems
people: Samit Dasgupta and Mahesh Kakde
explanation: Samit Dasgupta and Mahesh Kakde gave explicit p-adic formulas for number-theoretic building blocks associated with a broad family called totally real number fields. Their work supplies a p-adic version of part of Hilbert's 12th problem; Hilbert's original complex-number construction remains open in these cases.
whyItMatters: The result turns abstract existence into a recipe for constructing important extensions of number systems and advances a problem posed in 1900.
sourceTitle: Mathematicians find long-sought building blocks for special polynomials — Quanta Magazine

label: A mathematical story from 2022
title: A six-page proof explains sudden structure
people: Jinyoung Park and Huy Tuan Pham
explanation: When pieces are added at random, a property such as 'this network contains a loop through every vertex' can appear suddenly, almost like a switch. Park and Pham proved the Kahn–Kalai conjecture, showing that for a broad class of increasing properties in finite random sets, this threshold stays close to a simpler expectation estimate.
whyItMatters: Their remarkably short argument automatically settles many more specific threshold questions about random graphs and related structures.
sourceTitle: Jinyoung Park and Huy Tuan Pham prove the Kahn–Kalai conjecture — Stanford Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 2023
title: One tile that can never repeat
people: David Smith, Joseph Samuel Myers, Craig S. Kaplan and Chaim Goodman-Strauss
explanation: David Smith discovered the 'hat', and with Myers, Kaplan and Goodman-Strauss proved that copies of this one connected shape can cover the plane but can never form a repeating pattern. The hat's tilings use rotations and reflected copies; the same team later found the related 'spectre', which forces non-repetition without reflected copies.
whyItMatters: The discovery solved the long-standing one-tile problem and created a vivid link among geometry, logical proof, computation and mathematical art.
sourceTitle: An aperiodic monotile — Combinatorial Theory

demo.caption: The hat covers the plane only in non-repeating arrangements.

label: A mathematical story from 2024
title: A vast geometric translation dictionary is proved
people: Dennis Gaitsgory, Sam Raskin, Dima Arinkin, Dario Beraldo, Justin Campbell, Lin Chen, Joakim Færgeman, Kevin Lin and Nick Rozenblyum
explanation: A nine-person team released five papers proving the global, unramified geometric Langlands conjecture in its categorical form. In simpler terms, they built a rigorous translation dictionary between two very different ways of describing symmetry on curved surfaces; this does not settle every conjecture in the wider Langlands program.
whyItMatters: The proof combines more than 800 pages and about three decades of ideas, creating connections likely to influence geometry, representation theory, number theory and mathematical physics.
sourceTitle: Breakthrough in the Geometric Langlands program — Max Planck Institute for Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 2024
title: Infinitely many primes emerge from two prime squares
people: Ben Green and Mehtaab Sawhney
explanation: Green and Sawhney proved that, for suitable fixed values of n, infinitely many primes can be written as p² + nq² with p and q themselves prime. In particular, their work verifies the Friedlander–Iwaniec Gaussian-primes conjecture when n = 4.
whyItMatters: The theorem gives a precise count for a pattern involving primes inside a quadratic formula, using recent advances in additive combinatorics.
sourceTitle: Primes of the form p² + nq² — Ben Green and Mehtaab Sawhney

label: A mathematical story from 2025
title: The three-dimensional Kakeya conjecture is settled
people: Hong Wang and Joshua Zahl
explanation: Imagine a set in space that contains a unit-length needle pointing in every possible direction. Hong Wang and Joshua Zahl proved that every such Kakeya set in three-dimensional space has full Hausdorff and Minkowski dimension 3, even though its ordinary volume can be zero; higher-dimensional cases remain open.
whyItMatters: The result resolves the three-dimensional form of a 50-year-old problem whose geometry underpins difficult questions about waves, Fourier analysis and partial differential equations.
field: Geometric measure theory and harmonic analysis
sourceTitle: Volume estimates for unions of convex sets, and the Kakeya set conjecture in three dimensions — Hong Wang and Joshua Zahl

demo.caption: Rotate one unit segment through many directions while trying to keep the swept region small.

label: A mathematical story from 2025
title: A rigorous route from colliding particles to fluid equations
people: Yu Deng, Zaher Hani and Xiao Ma
explanation: Deng, Hani and Ma gave a rigorous derivation of major fluid equations from Newtonian systems of many colliding hard spheres, using the Boltzmann equation as the bridge between scales. Their preprint resolves the part of Hilbert's sixth problem covered by this dilute hard-sphere program under its stated regimes; it is not a claim about every possible fluid or physical model.
whyItMatters: The work mathematically connects microscopic particle collisions, statistical motion and the large-scale equations used to describe flowing gases.
field: Partial differential equations and mathematical physics
sourceTitle: Hilbert's sixth problem: derivation of fluid equations via Boltzmann's kinetic theory — Deng, Hani and Ma

label: Mathematics in 2026 so far
title: Four Fields Medals show mathematics' range
people: Yu Deng, John Pardon, Jacob Tsimerman and Hong Wang
explanation: At the 2026 International Congress of Mathematicians, the International Mathematical Union awarded Fields Medals to Yu Deng, John Pardon, Jacob Tsimerman and Hong Wang. Their cited work spans differential equations, geometry and topology, number theory, and harmonic analysis; this is a verified current-year event rather than a claim that one subjective 'biggest theorem' defines the unfinished year.
whyItMatters: The awards provide a current snapshot of the breadth of modern mathematics and recognise both outstanding existing work and the promise of future discoveries.
sourceTitle: Fields Medals 2026 — International Mathematical Union
